questions.stem: Which of the following best defines glocalisation?
options: Adapting a globally standardised product or marketing mix to suit local conditions
Marketing a product identically in every country
Producing only for the local market
Translating advertising into local languages
questions.why: The phrase worth remembering is think global, act local: keep the global brand and adapt what has to be adapted.
whyNot: That is a pure global marketing strategy.
That is domestic production.
Translation is one small part of adaptation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an ethnocentric marketing approach?
options: The home market's product and marketing are exported unchanged
Each country is treated as a separate market with its own product
A global strategy is combined with local adaptation
The product is designed for the largest foreign market
questions.why: It is cheap and treats foreign markets as an afterthought, which is why it so often fails.
whyNot: That is polycentric.
That is geocentric.
That is not one of the three named approaches.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a polycentric marketing approach?
options: Each country is treated as a separate market with its own product and marketing
The home offer is exported unchanged
A global strategy with local adaptation at the margin
Marketing is centralised at head office
questions.why: It fits each market best and forfeits scale economies and any consistent global brand.
whyNot: That is ethnocentric.
That is geocentric.
Centralisation describes structure, not this approach.

questions.stem: Where does selling an existing product in a new country sit in Ansoff's matrix?
options: Market development
Market penetration
Product development
Diversification
questions.why: Existing product, new market. It is the second-riskiest of the four options.
whyNot: Penetration means selling more of the same product in the same market.
Product development means a new product in the existing market.
Diversification means a new product in a new market.

questions.stem: Which elements of the marketing mix usually stay global?
options: The brand name, logo, core positioning and quality standards
Flavours, pack sizes and advertising imagery
Price points and distribution channels
Language and promotional media
questions.why: What usually adapts is the formulation, sizes, price points, channels and the execution of the message.
whyNot: Those are typically adapted.
Those are typically adapted.
Those are typically adapted.

questions.stem: Which of the following forces product adaptation whether the business wants it or not?
options: Local safety, labelling and ingredient regulation
A preference for the home country's advertising style
The business's own desire for scale economies
The existence of a trading bloc
questions.why: Regulation is a hard constraint, unlike a taste preference which the business could choose to ignore.
whyNot: That is an internal preference.
Scale economies argue against adaptation.
A bloc harmonises standards rather than forcing product change.

questions.stem: Why are smaller pack sizes used in lower-income markets?
options: They reach a lower price point while protecting the price per unit
They cost less per unit to produce
They are required by international standards
They avoid import tariffs
questions.why: Single-use sachets bring a product within reach of a daily rather than a monthly budget, which is adaptation of price and packaging rather than the product.
whyNot: Smaller packs usually cost more per unit to produce and package.
No such standard exists.
Tariffs depend on the goods, not the pack size.

questions.stem: Which element of the marketing mix differs most between countries?
options: Place, because retail structures and payment methods vary enormously
Product, because customers want the same things everywhere
Price, because currencies are convertible
Promotion, because advertising is globally standardised
questions.why: Reaching the customer is frequently the binding constraint, not persuading them.
whyNot: Tastes and regulation differ substantially.
Convertibility does not mean prices should be converted directly.
Advertising media and content regulation vary widely.

questions.stem: Why does adapting the product move a strategy towards diversification in Ansoff's terms?
options: The product is no longer the existing one, so both cost and risk rise
Adaptation changes the market rather than the product
Diversification always means entering a new country
Ansoff's matrix does not apply internationally
questions.why: It is a neat way of expressing the cost of glocalisation in a framework the examiner recognises.
whyNot: Adaptation changes the product; the market is already new.
Diversification means a new product in a new market.
It applies directly to global marketing decisions.

questions.stem: Why is a foreign entrant particularly exposed to being stuck in the middle?
options: It usually cannot beat local producers on cost and has not yet built enough brand to charge a premium
It is legally prevented from pursuing cost leadership
Porter's strategies do not apply to new entrants
It must always choose a focus strategy
questions.why: Naming that risk is a strong evaluative point in a global marketing question.
whyNot: No legal barrier applies.
They apply to any firm choosing a competitive basis.
Focus is often sensible but not compulsory.

questions.stem: Why does a focus strategy often suit market entry?
options: Serving an urban premium segment first and broadening later limits risk and cost
Focus strategies require no marketing spend
Narrow segments are always the most profitable
Focus avoids the need to understand the local culture
questions.why: It concentrates limited resources where the business is most likely to succeed before committing to the whole market.
whyNot: Targeted marketing still costs money.
Profitability depends on the segment and the competition.
Cultural understanding is still required.

questions.stem: What is the strongest reason for standardising a marketing mix globally?
options: Economies of scale in production and advertising, plus one consistent global brand
Local customers prefer foreign advertising
Standardisation guarantees regulatory compliance everywhere
It removes the need for market research
questions.why: Every adaptation costs money and loses some scale economy, so the test is whether it buys more extra revenue than it costs.
whyNot: Preferences vary and cannot be assumed.
Standardisation can breach local regulation.
Research is still needed to know what works.

questions.stem: Why is a single verdict on standardise-or-adapt usually a weak answer?
options: The answer differs by element of the mix, so each P needs its own judgement
Examiners never award marks for a conclusion
The two options are identical in practice
The mix cannot be separated into elements
questions.why: The product may standardise while the promotion and distribution must adapt, which is the move that lifts the answer.
whyNot: A judgement is required; it simply has to be differentiated.
They are materially different strategies.
The 4Ps are routinely considered separately.

questions.stem: Which approach do most large multinationals actually use?
options: Geocentric, standardising where they can and adapting where they must
Ethnocentric, exporting the home offer unchanged
Polycentric, designing everything separately for each country
None, because they market only in their home countries
questions.why: It is the honest answer to most questions in this topic.
whyNot: This is usually a sign of an inexperienced exporter.
It is too expensive and destroys brand consistency.
Multinationals by definition operate across countries.

questions.stem: Why must brand names be checked by native speakers in the target market?
options: A name can carry an unintended or offensive meaning in another language
Names must be legally registered in each language
Native speakers set the local price
Translation software cannot handle brand names
questions.why: Pronounceability and existing associations matter too: a name customers cannot say does not get recommended.
whyNot: Registration is a separate legal step.
Pricing is a commercial decision.
The issue is cultural meaning, not software capability.

questions.stem: Which product type standardises most successfully across countries?
options: Culturally neutral technology
Food and drink
Clothing and fashion
Media and entertainment
questions.why: Identifying what the product depends on should be the first step in a standardise-or-adapt answer.
whyNot: Food is among the most culturally sensitive categories.
Clothing is strongly affected by climate and culture.
Media depends heavily on language and cultural reference.
